utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the registrar would call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-04-82-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Appearances first for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, Your Honour, together with my colleague Joanne Motoike, Mr. Matthias Neuner, and our case manager Lakshima Walpita; and, just if I may, Your Honour, you may have heard that I'm less than 100 per cent healthy lately. I may leave this conference to a scheduled doctor's appointment with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you have my special understanding and sympathy having just got free of surgeons hands myself. Appearances then for Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Appearing for Mr. Boskoski, Guenal Mettraux, co-counsel; Edina Residovic, counsel; Jasenka Residovic, legal assistant and case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. And for Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. Mr. Johan Tarculovski, Antonio Apostolski, lead counsel; and Mr. Jordan Apostolski, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. May I once again welcome counsel, and inquire now whether each accused are receiving a translation that is enabling them to follow the proceedings. Is that so, first of all, Mr. Boskoski? THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. We get translation. We are able to follow the procedure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Tarculovski. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] I also, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, we are sitting today for a further Status Conference in this case, having regard to the plan that would enable a start to this case in the next month. May I commence by apologising to all that it is not been possible to issue decisions in a number of motions that are presently before the Chamber. The essence of the delay is in the appointment of the actual Chamber to conduct the case. I've just within the last hour spoken to the President, and he hopes to have responses from New York that will enable him to make the final appointments, he hopes by the end of this week. Once those appointments are made, there are drafts ready on nearly all the decisions and the other is imminent so that we could have a great flood of decisions happening very shortly, and that, I know, will enable, then, all counsel to prepare with greater certainty and greater awareness of what it is that they will be dealing with in the way of witnesses, exhibits, experts and the like. I regret that it has just been this administrative difficulty. It's been complicated by unexpected happenings in other trials, which have put into question how the Trial Chamber for this case would be constituted. Those issues have been resolved, and we simply wait on decision from New York to enable the appointment. So I hope that explanation will assist you to understand, and that had it will be possible for you to continue with the orderly preparation of your case without too much disturbance because of this unexpected delay. Now, there was an issue, I think, affecting Mr. Apostolski in particular, concerning an assistant counsel. Are you able to indicate whether that matter is nearing resolution?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this issue will be resolved maybe during this very day, because we are awaiting a confirmation from co-counsel, Jasmina Zivkovic, for her to be confirmed as a co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. I think the nature of the trial will be one that will require a -- quite a bit of work in a fairly confined time, and I think that a second counsel will make a big difference to your capacity to deal with the demands of the trial. When we were last at a Status Conference, there was pending an issue concerning the languages at the trial. I understand that in the meantime it has been possible for administrative arrangements to be made that will enable a B/C/S translation, as well as the translations we were expecting of Macedonian, Albanian, French, and English. So as long as we don't get witnesses from other countries, we will be able, I hope now, to enable all participants to follow the proceedings with ready convenience. There appears to still be a few issues to be finalised concerning the preparation of documents by all parties, especially in their translation. I wonder, Mr. Saxon, whether you would be able to bring me up to date on that, from your point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Your Honour, the -- from the Prosecution's perspective, we are fully in compliance with our obligation according to the practice of this Tribunal to provide all of our Rule 65 ter exhibit to the accused in a language that they understand. That work is now complete. With regard to translations from Macedonian or other languages into English, there are still some documents on the Prosecution's exhibit list that CLSS is still working on, but I'm optimistic that between now and the start of the trial these document will be available to us in English so there -- there is no issue ever any delay in the start of the trial. I would like to clarify something that I noticed by reading the transcript of yesterday's Rule 65 ter Conference, and I believe before I went home ill yesterday, I managed to confuse my co-counsel, Ms. Motoike, which then perhaps caused some concern with my learned colleagues regarding to the issue of certain translations, and it's simply this. It's regarding the Prosecution's position concerning source materials for the expert report of Viktor Bezruchenko who is the Prosecution's military analyst in this case. And as you are probably aware, Your Honour, the Prosecution just out of a sense of order and completeness placed all of that source material at the end of its first amended exhibit list. There was a brief discussion yesterday afternoon, I noticed, regarding the Prosecution's translation obligations for such -- for such documents. As Mr. Mettraux rightly pointed out, any documents which the Prosecution tenders in this case will be translated into English, one of the official languages of this Tribunal. And as I said before, that process is well under way now by CLSS. The practice of the ICTY requires exhibits on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list to be translated into the language of the accused; in this case, Macedonian. All the exhibits on the Prosecution's first amended exhibit list, with the exception of some exhibits that are source material to Viktor Bezruchenko's expert report, have been translated into Macedonian and disclosed to the Defence. In this case, several hundred pages of source materials to Viktor Bezruchenko's expert report are in English, and the Prosecution's position has been for the past year that it is not required to translate such material into Macedonian, although much of the material quite frankly is in the original Macedonian language. However, to facilitate the work of the Defence, the Prosecution has translated to date and disclosed approximately 75 per cent of this source material from English into Macedonian, and it is endeavouring to complete this process as soon as possible. Certainly it will be complete well before Mr. Bezruchenko testifies in this case, if he is permitted to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Saxon. And especially your clarification about that source material so that the translations are being completed and would be available before the witness is called. Thank you. Ms. Residovic, is there anything, any issue concerning translations of material that you wish to report or to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have just heard the explanation, and we are satisfied that all the documents on the Prosecutor's list will be also be translated into the working language of the Court, but also the language of the accused. That was a question that remained open yesterday. As for other issues, the documents which we intend to use in the course of the proceedings, either exhibit -- as exhibits or for cross-examination purposes, will be translated in the usual way through the Tribunal service; and in spite of the best efforts of the CLSS, we are still experiencing significant problems. However, I believe that with the support of the Court if priority is given to Defence documents as well, we will be able to complete the process successfully by the start of trial or at least by the time we need to use the documents. In our communication with the Prosecutor's office concerning other issues such as agreeing to the authenticity of exhibits, it will be important for us to be informed who is translating the documents, because many of the documents we receive from the Prosecutor, as a Prosecutor himself as confirmed, were not translated by CLSS, but have been translated by persons unknown to us. In order for us to evaluate the authenticity of documents, we wish to know the source, or rather, the person or persons engaged in translating the documents. These are the questions we have, and the problems we are running into as concerns translations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I may just briefly respond, because Ms. Residovic touched on an issue that I wanted to raise anyway today. The Prosecution does not understand clearly what the connection is between the authenticity of a document and the question of who translates that document from one language into another. It seems to the Prosecution that these are two very separate issues. The -- the accused Boskoski or counsel for accused Boskoski has inquired, I think, at least twice now to the Prosecution as to which of the exhibits on its exhibit list have been translated into English by persons other than members of CLSS or staff of CLSS, and the Prosecution has provided Defence counsel with a list of those exhibits that have been translated not by CLSS but by employees of the OTP itself. If the Defence want to challenge the accuracy or sufficiency or clarity of any such translations, we ask the Defence to notify the Prosecution immediately so that we can hopefully discuss these issues, review the translations that the Defence has concerns about, if necessary, obtain a revised translation. But for obvious reasons, we would like to address these issues and hopefully resolve them now prior to the start of the trial than after the witnesses are beginning to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I indicate for your assistance, Ms. Residovic, that from the point of view of the practice of the Tribunal, the obligation is to provide a translated document. The concern you have about the identity of a particular translator is not one that is the subject of any rule nor of any practice of the Tribunal, and it would not be a basis for a challenge to the translation simply that this was a particular document which was translated by person X or person Y. What is the established practice is that if a party considers that a translation provided is not accurate, then the party may dispute the accuracy of that translation. I understand from what has occurred, and from Mr. Saxon's explanation, that you have been informed which documents, in fact, are translations prepared by staff of the OTP and which documents are translated by the Tribunal's translation service. That cooperation will enable you perhaps to focus your attention if you have any concerns that the translations may be less than adequate. But really, it's for you, if you are concerned, to challenge the accuracy of a translation and to indicate the basis for your concern. That being made clear, as long as Mr. Saxon continues to assist you by letting you know which documents are those of the translation service and which are prepared by ours, then I really don't think that the Chamber would have any further interest in the matter, and it would be entirely for you, if you are concerned about a particular translation, then to raise that perhaps first with the Prosecution, but then there is no satisfaction certainly to raise it with the Chamber. Thank you for that. Now, if I could ask you, Mr. Apostolski, whether there are any issues that affect you or concern you about the matter of translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in respect to the translations, we may inform the Court that we are in the process of translating our documents that have been submitted by the CLSS. The only thing I would like to ask the Court is to accelerate the translation procedure, to make it as fast as possible, because we need those documents in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wish I had a magic wand, Mr. Apostolski. But the problem is there are a certain number of translators who must deal with the needs of this case, which is the only Macedonian case, and I know that they are working at the limits of their capacity. Now, the consequence of that is that not all documents can be available now. The service is well aware of the date planned for the start of the trial, and I know they are giving their best efforts to try to ensure that the documents are available by then. So I'm afraid we must accept that there are some limitations on the capacity to provide the translation of the very significant number of documents that are concerned when we're dealing with a language that is not one of the authorised languages of the Tribunal. So we expect to get there but I can't just say, Work harder. They are working hard now. Well, thank you for that. Disclosure, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Rule 66(A)(ii), the Prosecution is up to date. With respect to Rule 66(B), as I explained before, the Prosecution is also up to date, including with respect to translations. With respect to the Prosecution's disclosure obligations pursuant to Rule 68, as you know, that process is ongoing and will be ongoing throughout these proceedings. The Prosecution has commenced its so-called updated electronic searches of its evidentiary collections based on the search criteria that it has been using for the past 18 months. The trial team is begun reviewing the results of these searches and commenced disclosure of material that has been identified as following within the scope of Rule 68. At the last Status Conference in December, the Prosecution asked the Defence to review the search criteria to see if they were all still necessary, in the hopes that if some of these search criteria could be dropped, the workload could be reduced for both parties. The Prosecution did not receive any response from the Defence and, therefore, these updated searches are continuing as initially planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When does that mean that they will finish, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot give you a precise date because this work depends on a particular unit of the Prosecution, of the OTP, that is performing these searches, and this is not the only case for which these searches are performed. But it is my understanding that this set of updated searches will be completed during the spring, certainly well before the trial is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not a very encouraging statement, Mr. Saxon. To be told in the closing stages of a trial that some documents have just been discovered or a new witness has just been identified when that information was known to the Prosecution before the trial commenced, well, that perhaps not identified for relevance can be productive of a great deal of difficulty and inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I take Your Honour's point. With your leave, may I have your permission to consult with the unit that is performing the searches and perhaps get a more fixed deadline from them, and I will report that at the Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I also inquire do I take it answer that the present Rule 68 material that has been identified that that has already been translated. Is that what you're saying? Sorry, I'm wrong there. That any Rule 68 material that is known and has been identified has been the subject of appropriate notice to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And this process began actually in early Autumn of 2005 and is continuing to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any disclosure issue that concerns either Defence. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the last Status Conference, the OTP has provided us with 16 batches with new documents, new witness statements, new experts, and also these batches contain the answers to some questions that the Defence asked the Prosecution. After five and a half years of investigation, less than a month before the start of trial, the OTP should finally make it possible for to us know that we do have all the statements, all the witnesses, all the document disclosed to us, because, Your Honours, we are preparing on the basis of the witness lists and the documents that the OTP has disclosed to the Defence to date. As for 68 -- Rule 68 disclosure, it's true that the Prosecutor has submitted to us a list of key words which they used to search the material, and they have disclosed over 30.000 documents to us. But as we have already submitted to the Trial Chamber a motion under Rule 68, it is our position that the fact that the OTP has conducted the search according to selected key words does not satisfy the Prosecutor's obligation to establish whether these documents truly meet the criteria of Rule 68 in our case, as regards the counts in the indictment. For this reason we submitted our motion and the arguments that we have submitted. I do not wish to repeat those arguments now because the Office of the Prosecutor will probably respond to those in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an answer to the question that you asked several moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We do the best we can, Your Honour, probably not quick enough but ... It is excepted that these updated searches, in other words, the second round of such searches, will be completed within the next three weeks, and after that we'll -- we'll need some time for the Prosecution team to review the results of the searches to see if there is any material disclosable under Rule 68 contained within it. But it shouldn't then be too far from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after the discussions with several of the witnesses for whom we believe that they might be beneficial for the accused, we ascertained that those have been interrogated by the OTP. Considering that those statements were not disclosed by the OTP, we have asked the OTP to respond upon that motion. So in the direct correspondence with my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, we agreed that we would indicate more precisely the names of those witnesses and it's OTP should respond on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. And I could observe that seems to be a very practical approach. The range of potential material that has to be examined for Rule 68 is quite enormous; and if you're concerned about particular matters for you to raise that specifically with the Prosecutor, enables attention to be focused and ought to ensure that you get the results that you need much more quickly. So thank you, indeed, for that. Now, I have mentioned that the Chamber, as presently constituted is well aware of the number of pending motions, in particular the 92 bis and 92 ter motions that are pending, and the motions concerning expert witnesses and exhibits. And as I've indicated, as soon as the composition of the final -- the final composition of the Trial Chamber to actually conduct the trial is formalised, it is anticipated that decisions will issue very quickly. With that in mind, I wouldn't propose to go through any of those pending motions at this hearing, unless any party sees that there is a particular need to raise any one or more of them. I leave that open in case there is some matter that you feel needs to be mentioned. So first Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the sake of clarity, it's simply my obligation to notify the Chamber of an error that I noticed in one of these Prosecution's motions just this morning. It is in annex D to the Prosecution's third revised motion for admission of written statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Annex D.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: D as in Daniel, and the error is that simply that in there annex D, for the name Bolton, the Prosecution noted that the witness should not appear for cross-examination, and also that the witness would be -- witness' written statements would be fully subjected to Rule 92 bis. That contradicts what the Prosecution said in the narrative of its motion, and that was an error, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So is it the narrative to be preferred to the annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The narrative is the correct legal position, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Is there any particular matter concerning motions that you feel should be raised, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we simply wish to reiterate what we said yesterday at the 65 ter Conference; that is, that the Defence does not oppose colour pictures being replaced by black and white photographs. That was the last motion by the OTP, although if -- if Your Honours feel that we must submit our response in writing, we will do so, but, otherwise, I hope this can be considered our consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for indicating that, and I am sure that that can be accepted as a sufficient response by you at this stage. There is no advantage to be gained by unnecessary formality of written documents, so any time you wish to indicate your agreement to something for any party that can be done orally at this stage. That will save time an effort for all parties concerned. Mr. Apostolski, any matter you wish to raise about the motions?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not, Your Honour, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I noticed today that we continue to get a quite a number of fresh motions day by day. I hope the enthusiasm of the parties is just about at an end, if we're to cope with the volume that is there. We want to have these matters finalised and in order, if we can, before the commencement date. Is there any other issue which any party feels ought to be raised at this time? Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have a few, Your Honour, if I can indulge your patience for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I may, if you could ask counsel for Mr. Tarculovski to clarify something that I read in the transcript of yesterday's 65 ter meeting, and the need for clarification is this: At pages 327 to 328 of the transcript, counsel for Mr. Tarculovski explained that the accused Tarculovski would agree to the authenticity of a number of Prosecution exhibits. And at least in the English translation, that was the word that was used more than once, "authenticity." And the reason this is important to the Prosecution is in a letter from the 31st of January of this year, which counsel for Mr. Tarculovski sent to the Prosecution, counsel for Tarculovski stated that they would agree to the admissibility of a group of proposed Prosecution exhibits. And, obviously, there is a significant legal difference between the concept of agreeing to this authenticity versus the admissibility of the exhibit itself. And we would just like -- we would just want to know if counsel for the accused Tarculovski could indicate whether they are changing their position laid out in the letter of 31 January, or does it remain the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Are you able to assist us there, Mr. Apostolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In respect to this issue, we will respond in writing. As I mentioned to my learned colleague the Prosecutor, we are constantly making efforts to establish the non-disputable facts, and we still remain the possibility open to have some fact that this is indisputable and to accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When do you think Mr. Saxon might receive your written indication of your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are reviewing certain points of the indictment, so in the matter of two weeks we will be able to inform the OTP on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It would be of assistance if you could provide a copy of that advice to the Chamber as well when you are in a position give it to Mr. Saxon, Mr. Apostolski. And you indicated there was more than one matter, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, there was, Your Honour. I understand that yesterday the question arose whether the Prosecution intended to stand by or change its prior estimate of the time needed for the Prosecution's case in chief. And I would just like to tell the Trial Chamber that at this time we stand by our prior estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Subject to 92 bis, 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you for that qualification, that is a very important qualifications, Your Honour. Subject to the decisions of the Trial Chamber on these motions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So your estimate is based on the acceptance of your motions in full, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also like to inform the Chamber and the parties that the Prosecution within the next two weeks will probably file a short addendum to the expert report of its military analyst, Viktor Bezruchenko, and this short addendum will be based on documents recently received from the government of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, finally, Your Honour, as you may have heard already, the Prosecution has produced what it refers to as a panorama exhibit of the village of Ljuboten itself and surrounding important landmarks that are relevant to the second amended indictment, and the Prosecution has prepared this visual aid to assist not only the Prosecution but also, if they wish, the Defence and the Trial Chamber at trial, because this effectively would give all parties before the Court the opportunity to show witnesses whether on direct exam or cross-examination virtually a three-dimensional perspective of particular locations that will be discussed during the trial. The Prosecution has prepared what it refers to as a court binder of still photographs of, again, important locations that are related to the allegations in the indictment, and the Prosecution would simply ask perhaps for a moment or two of time at the Pre-Trial Conference on the 12th of April to show these visual aids to the Chamber and the Defence, in the hopes that the parties can agree that they can be used at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Saxon, I think we would all understand that any visual or other aid to understanding evidence more clearly is always welcome, but obviously the nature of the two items that you have identified is such that it ought to be the subject of disclosure to both Defence teams beforehand, so that all parties can be assured of the reliability of what you have produced, and it will then be of assistance to the Chamber, if that is the position reached. So your plan that these should be ready and able to be viewed by the Defence teams and the Chamber at the Pre-Trial Conference is, I think, a very sensible and welcome one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We actually -- excuse me, the Prosecution showed Defence counsel an early version of both visual aids yesterday, but we will endeavour to finalise both aids and provide copies to counsel prior to the 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Residovic, is there any other matter that you wish to raise at this time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't have any issues to raise. We would just like to repeat what our position is. We believe that the OTP has to provide with us a final list of evidence and witnesses because the trial is just about to start; and as has been outlined in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief, the case is as it has been outlined and as it has been outlined by the pre-trial brief of the Defence. Any new disclosure provided to us by the OTP as technical solutions or new evidence have to go through a certain procedure allowing the Defence to state their position on the admissibility of such documents. I would like to thank the Registry for their understanding, which has resulted in the use of various languages during the trial and the assistance that has been provided to the Defence by the Trial Chamber. I would also like to thank the OTP and their case managers who will by the 3rd of April provide us with EDS version of the evidence that we previously had on CDs. This will allow the Defence to search using different criterias not only the ones we could use for CDs. The Defence does not have any other issues to raise at today's Status Conference. We were in constant contact with the OTP and together we will try to resolve any outstanding issues. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully support my colleague Edina Residovic, especially with regards to the motion to the Prosecutor's office to prepare the final list of witnesses that will -- those that will be nominated by the OTP. And I think that in coordination between us and the OTP, if there are other issues, we will resolve them through direct agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed, Mr. Apostolski. I understand, Mr. Saxon, that you are advising the Defence of the first, was it 15 witnesses that you intend to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. We have advised them of our list of the first 15 witnesses, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. I think that is a very useful step at this point allowing a more orderly preparation. Thank you. Well, there is no other matter which the Chamber sees as requiring attention. Could I raise with either Mr. Boskoski or Mr. Tarculovski, have any personal issue they wish to raise about the case? Mr. Boskoski. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] I don't have any, Your Honour. I don't have any issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tarculovski. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Me neither, Your Honour, I don't have any issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed. Well, may I thank counsel then for their attendance and assistance, and we plan next to sit on the 12th of April for the Pre-Trial Conference. So unless something unexpected occurs, we will convene again at that time to consider the final state of the case for trial. Thank you indeed. We are now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at.
